extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry/practical criticism; readers learning to evaluate poems
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and evaluation of lyric poems, emphasising imagery, diction, sound, movement, tone, and reader-response; guidance aimed at teaching practical criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting figurative language and hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers are often at a loss when required to interpret and judge figurative language (hyperbole, emotive similes) and need guidance on proper approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that hyperbole and emotive similes may not be literally true; avoid forcing literal readings. See Part III, Chapter 2 for fuller discussion (page note). Examples in the chunk show readers misinterpreting or over-literalising similes and hyperbole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing emotive vs elucidatory similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some similes are emotive (suggest feeling) rather than elucidatory (clarify meaning), and must be judged accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand that every simile explain or create a literal picture; assess whether an emotive simile properly contributes to tone or feeling rather than literal intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery's effectiveness in producing mental pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: A test of a poem's imagery is whether the reader forms a mental picture from the poet's words — if the picture arises, the poem may be judged good by that standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the verbal image successfully evokes stable mental imagery. Be aware that vivid images can be personally idiosyncratic; a strong visual response in one reader is not universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images as amplifiers of quality (make good better, bad worse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images tend to magnify the reader's pre-existing response: they 'make good better and bad worse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that effective imagery can elevate a poem, but erratic or unsuitable imagery can fatally hinder a reader's appreciation; consider how images interact with the poem's base quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images as indicators of reader engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Images are often best regarded as signs of how the reader is getting on with the poem, not necessarily as means the poet uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use readers' visualisations diagnostically: vivid imagery may indicate absorption, but the distance between verbal figure and visual image and readers' idiosyncrasies mean images are unreliable as proof of poetic intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's uncontrolled visualising and misreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' uncontrolled visualization (e.g., imagining a cloud with a pencil) can produce irrelevant or misleading interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in treating a reader's spontaneous visual detail as a critique of the poem; distinguish between what the poet suggests and what the reader's mind invents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction must suit the picture (word-picture correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poet paints a word-picture, the choice of words should accord with the intended picture (delicate pictures require light words; heavy pictures require weighty words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether particular words (e.g., 'miraculous', 'encroachments', 'beneficence') harmonise with the poem's intended effect or break the image; beware that readers' judgements of 'light' vs 'cumbrous' words are subjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing incompatible diction registers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing delicate and cumbrous words or disparate registers (Latin/Anglo‑Saxon mix, prosaic with lofty diction) can blur or break the poem's picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for consistency of diction appropriate to the poem's aims; note when abrupt register shifts produce a sense of artificiality or bathos (examples: 'stockade' with delicate imagery; sudden grandiloquence in later stanzas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate sound (alliteration, sibilance, cacophony) in context
rubrics_metrics.description: No sound in poetry can be judged apart from its place and function in the poem; euphony or cacophony must be assessed in the whole design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist applying external, arbitrary canons of 'ugly' sounds; consider how alliteration, consonant clusters, and sibilants operate within the poem's lines and overall effect (e.g., 'Climb, cloud' or repeated s sounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Onomatopoeia and sound imitation rarely confer merit by themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Most alleged instances of onomatopoeia are imaginary and onomatopoeia alone never gave a line of verse poetic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overvalue simple sound-imitations; assess sound as part of diction, rhythm, and meaning rather than as an isolated quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between verse movement and subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may imitate the motion of his subject by the motion of his verse; this is a merit if required by his purpose, but not a defect if absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether matching movement (rhythm, metre) to subject matter serves the poem's purpose; avoid prescribing that subject must always determine metrical motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegitimacy of prescribing means (expecting fixed technical correspondences)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is illegitimate to demand a fixed correspondence (e.g., 'cloud' must have flowing verse); prescribing means confuses poetry with parlour games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow poets freedom of means; only criticise mismatches when it's clear the poet intended correspondence and failed to fulfil that purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary canons (imperfect rhyme test, fixed euphony rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying simple, external tests (like imperfect-rhyme or hard-consonant bans) without entering into the poem is foolish and misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require critics to examine lines in their precise context and resist checklist-style rejections based on isolated features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest/emotion not required of all poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The complaint 'the poem is dead because it wants in human interest' mistakes a prescriptive demand; poetry need not always present overt human interest to be valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different poems aim at different responses (vivid description, philosophical reflection, rapture); do not conflate intensity of experience with poetic quality or require 'rapture' from every poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of tone and register (avoid abrupt stylistic shifts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden changes of manner or register (e.g., delicate imagery followed by grandiloquent diction) can break unity and mislead readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether transitions (tone, diction, stanza form) are deliberate and justified; if they are accidental or discordant, they may produce anti-climax or resentment (examples: stanza 6's entry of 'pomp', 'beneficence').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bathos and ludicrous endings
rubrics_metrics.description: An anti-climactic or ludicrous conclusion ('O most lame and impotent conclusion!') undermines a poem that had earlier succeeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for weakening in final stanzas due to inappropriate diction or argument (vocatives, feeble questions), and critique whether the poem sustains its earlier effects to the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical and physical plausibility of images
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurities or apparent physical impossibilities (e.g., 'shake your shadow at the sun') invite reader complaint and require careful interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple interpretations (literal cloud shaking vs shadow movement via sea); where physical reading fails, ask whether metaphorical or poetic sense rescues the line before condemning it as error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensibility vs intended obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poems may initially seem obscure and require prolonged study; lack of immediate understanding is not necessarily a defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between genuine obscurity (confused expression) and complexity that rewards attention. Avoid dismissing poems that ask for careful reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging single words out of context (subjectivity of 'prosaic'/'ugly')
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'prosaic', 'ugly', or 'cumbrous' are often subjective and serve as terms of abuse when used without contextual argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific reasons when labelling words prosaic; remember that words disliked by some readers may be felicitous to others — critique should focus on function within the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader preconceptions as obstacles to fair reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical preconceptions (doctrines applied crudely) or moral/political biases can obstruct a reader's engagement and lead to illegitimate condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and bracket personal preconceptions (e.g., demands for 'human interest' or moralising expectations) when evaluating a poem; check whether an objection stems from an outside doctrine rather than the poem itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish intensity of experience from poetic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusing the intensity of a reader's emotion (rapture, anger, boredom) with the intrinsic quality of the poem leads to inconsistent judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the poem on its formal and imaginative merits as well as its emotional impact; do not reduce critical judgment to whether the poem arouses violent feeling in the critic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and stanza structure should serve meaning and transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in stanzaic form (e.g., four-line to three-line stanzas) can mark thematic or tonal transitions and should be noticed and evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how form signals shifts (example: change at verse 9 marking reminiscence) and whether form-change is effectively timed and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vocative/imperative address influences reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Vocative or imperative modes ('O sprawling domes', 'Climb, cloud') can provoke strong reader responses and may be judged as amateurish or effective depending on execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether direct address fits the poem's tone and purpose; if vocatives create unintended parody or bathos, note this as a fault of register or aim.
